title: Unlocking Scientific Concepts: How Effective Are LLM-Generated Analogies for Student Understanding and Classroom Practice?
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’25)
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language model (LLM)-generated analogies can support understanding of scientific concepts in K-12 education and how teachers can use and adapt such analogies in real classroom practice. The authors focus on two related questions: first, whether analogies generated by GPT-4o improve student problem solving when students use them without teacher intervention; and second, what teachers need from such analogies and how effective they are when teachers integrate them into instruction.

The study uses a two-stage design in a Chinese high school. In Study I, 49 ninth-grade students completed an in-class test on unfamiliar physics and biology concepts, comparing a textbook-only condition with a textbook-plus-LLM-analogy condition. The researchers measured answer accuracy and self-confidence and also interviewed a subset of students. In Study II, the authors interviewed two teachers and two senior students to derive requirements for classroom use, then conducted a one-week field study in two first-year high school classes where two teachers used LLM-generated analogies in one class and regular instruction in the other.

The paper finds that LLM-generated analogies can help with some biology concepts, but their effectiveness is inconsistent across subjects and can also produce overconfidence and occasional misunderstanding when students rely on incomplete or erroneous analogies. In the classroom study, teachers were able to refine analogies, discard unnecessary ones, and use them in ways that matched their instructional goals; the analogies were most useful when they were vivid, aligned with subject needs, and focused on key parts of a concept rather than trying to explain everything. The authors conclude that current LLM-generated analogies are not well suited for unsupervised student self-learning, but can be useful as teacher-facing preparation tools when combined with teacher judgment and modification.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study using a controlled in-class comparison plus a qualitative field study, but it is not a full randomized controlled trial with strong causal controls across settings. The evidence base is mixed-method and locally bounded to one high school, so credibility is moderate rather than high.
impact_tier_rationale: The findings suggest some positive effects on biology concept understanding and student confidence, but effects were inconsistent across subjects and sometimes negative due to over-reliance and missing information. Overall impact is modest and unclear for general K-12 use rather than clearly large or broadly transferable.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated analogies for science concept explanation and teacher lesson preparation/refinement in high school biology and physics; GPT-4o was used to generate, revise, and select analogies for classroom use.

finding.finding_summary: In a controlled in-class test with valid data from 44 students (n=22 per group), LLM-generated analogies improved understanding for some biology concepts but not physics overall. The paper reports a significant association between group and accuracy for biology (exact Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney p=0.042), while physics showed no significant benefit; confidence ratings also increased significantly for both subjects, indicating stronger subjective understanding without consistent accuracy gains.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice concept question accuracy and 5-point self-confidence ratings on four unfamiliar science concepts
finding.study_size: n=44 valid test papers (22 textbook-only, 22 textbook+LLM analogy)

finding.finding_summary: In the one-week classroom field study, teachers reported that LLM-generated analogies were useful for teaching key points, stimulating interest, and supporting classroom understanding when they were selectively edited to fit lesson goals. The evidence is qualitative rather than effect-size based, but teachers observed better classroom feedback and homework performance in the analogy condition relative to usual practice.
finding.measure: Teacher observations, student feedback, and reported homework/classroom performance during 12 lessons

finding.finding_summary: Student self-confidence was higher when LLM-generated analogies were provided, but this did not reliably translate into better accuracy. The paper also notes overconfidence and over-reliance on analogies, suggesting the tool can increase perceived understanding while sometimes weakening calibration.
finding.measure: 5-point self-confidence ratings; interview evidence of overconfidence/over-reliance
finding.study_size: n=44 valid test papers; 8 interviewed students
